activities.caption: rank the levers the way practice does
activities.name: ct2HierOrder

config.prompt: Practice ranks the three dimensions — assemble the hierarchy:
items: Value — lightness versus darkness, independent of hue
Hue — which colour, the wheel position
config.why: A painting with correct values and wrong hues still reads (a Monet in greyscale still organises); wrong values fail no matter how refined the hues. Tint, shade and tone are just value travels along one hue.

config.text: Three cone types explain why three primaries suffice; Hering's %%0%% explains the phenomena artists see — there is no 'reddish green', staring at red produces a %%1%% afterimage, and colour constancy %%2%% so a white shirt looks white in tungsten or daylight.
config.hint: One names the wiring, one the afterimage colour, one what the brain does to the light source.

activities.anchor: The trap lives in the difference
activities.caption: additive or subtractive? file the mixing facts
activities.name: ct2MixSort

items.label: all three light primaries together = white
each pigment absorbs part of the spectrum; the residue reaches the eye
printing runs on CMY(K) — magenta + yellow make red

config.why: Mix more, subtract more — and the traditional painter's R-Y-B wheel gives different complements than the physical ones: on a printer's wheel, red's partner is cyan, not green.

activities.caption: one line of this colour-system summary is wrong
activities.name: ct2PrimSpot

config.prompt: One line of this colour-system summary is wrong — click it:
lines: Screens mix red, green and blue light additively.
Printers mix cyan, magenta and yellow subtractively.
Red, yellow and blue are the one true master set of primaries.
The painter's R-Y-B wheel is an eighteenth-century convention.
On the printer's wheel, red's partner is cyan, not green.
config.correction: Primaries are chosen per system — there is no master set, only the set that fits the medium you are mixing in.
config.why: Every designer who has watched a screen-perfect RGB palette collapse in CMYK print has met gamut — the set of colours a device can physically produce — the hard way.

activities.anchor: the electric red-on-green of van Gogh
activities.caption: judged in isolation vs judged in situ
activities.name: ct2AlbersCompare

config.prompt: One colour, two judging conditions — drag the divider:

before.label: in isolation
before.text: a swatch chosen on white, or matched from memory — with no field, there is nothing to calibrate against

after.label: in situ
after.text: the same swatch against its field — simultaneous contrast has already shifted its value and temperature, so only the relationship on the canvas is real

config.why: Albers's meta-lesson: colour is 'the most relative medium in art' — you do not choose colours, you choose conditions, and the viewer's eye finishes the job. The Bezold effect and metamerism extend the same relativity to patterns and lighting.

activities.anchor: a scheme is a hierarchy, not a democracy
activities.caption: match each scheme to its trade
activities.name: ct2SchemeMatch

config.prompt: The wheel as a relationship menu — match scheme to what it buys:

pairs.right: maximum contrast for accents and focal points — and mixed, the most natural neutrals and shadows
instant harmony — needs value or temperature contrast to separate elements
complementary energy with less shout and more nuance
vivid balance that wants one hue dominant

config.why: Two disciplines apply to all schemes: dominance (the 60-30-10 habit) and the limited palette — three pigments plus white, whose mixtures harmonise automatically because they share ancestry.

config.prompt: Roughly what percentage of men have red-green colour vision deficiency?
config.why: About 8% of men and 0.5% of women — so hue alone must never carry meaning: pair every hue distinction with a value or shape distinction. The same value-first rule, wearing a design-systems badge.
config.context: about 8% of men, 0.5% of women — value redundancy is free accessibility

config.prompt: Four wheels, one lineage — assemble it:
items: Newton's 1704 wheel — physics: spectral hues bent into a circle, purple as the mixture the spectrum lacks
Goethe's 1810 Theory of Colours — psychology: afterimages, contrast, the felt temperature of hues
The Bauhaus — Itten's seven contrasts as curriculum, Albers's relativity exercises as corrective
config.why: Itten taught colour as universal law; Albers taught it as context-dependent experience — modern practice blends them: schemes give the starting hypothesis, the interaction effects decide in situ.
